LGF.text:
- Mitochondrial and cellular energy starvation (glutamine, butyrate, TCA intermediates): your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, right there in the gut and right away, to keep its tight junctions intact, so if the cells lining your small intestine (called enterocytes) or your large intestine (colonocytes) don't get the fuels their mitochondria prefer, the barrier structurally breaks down, and lipopolysaccharides (LPS, which come from the walls of bacteria) and other endotoxins leak through into your bloodstream.

    - L-Glutamine ([watch Dr. Rhonda vid](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=5DVUEKrekYw&ra=m)) is the top fuel for those small intestine cells, and for your immune cells when they're activated. It skips the complicated digestive steps and gets turned directly into alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG) inside the mitochondria, where it powers the citric acid cycle (the cycle mitochondria use to make energy), so the cells get that energy right away, and that's what drives the repair of the gut lining and stops LPS from getting through.

      - Take 5g a day as a baseline. That's to counter the breakdown of the gut lining you get from high-intensity or high-volume training (like CrossFit or intense cardio). Then raise it gradually to 10-30g a day when your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, when your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis).

      - CAUTION: cancer cells that multiply really fast can also hijack glutamine to fuel their growth, so don't raise it to the high doses if you have an active colon or liver cancer (the liver gets the glutamine first, through the portal vein).

    - Butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): the small intestine runs on glutamine, but the large intestine runs on SCFAs like butyrate. You get those when your gut bacteria ferment raw resistant starch, or from your home-brewed SIBO yogurt, and they fuel the cells of your colon and lock down the lower gut barrier. They also keep turning down inflammatory signals.

    - TCA cycle intermediates (malic and citric acid): organic acids like malate and citrate feed directly into the same energy pathways in the mitochondria that glutamine does, so clean sour stuff (like organic malic acid, tart cherries or green apples) gives your gut cells a quick alternative fuel, which speeds up healing of the lining from a different biochemical angle.

ST1.text:
## Optional Ready-Made Gut Stacks

I don't think there's one universal supplement stack that heals everyone's gut, but the order you do things in does matter. You fix the mechanics of digestion first (Phase 1), then reset your diet and motility (Phase 2), and you only move on to antimicrobial or anti-parasite protocols if you still have symptoms after that (Phase 3).

But some people would rather have a ready-made starting point than buy every ingredient separately. For a general "repair and rebuild" approach, I'd look for a stack that covers three things: something for your microbiome (a probiotic or a probiotic system that you tolerate well), something that helps your gut make short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate (that's the prebiotic or butyrate support), and something that repairs the barrier (nutrients for the gut lining like glutamine, zinc carnosine, colostrum, mucosal-support herbs or similar compounds).
ST1.notes: Claude, E338: the order said in full with the phase each step is (a pointer of mine, for him to approve); the three categories said as what each does for you.

ST2.text:
Gemini suggested these kits to me, but so far they're the best ones I've seen, tho I haven't used them myself, so check the reviews. The best general one is Microbiome Labs Total Gut Restoration, because it has all three parts in it: probiotic, prebiotic and mucosal support. If you're dealing with leaky gut more specifically, Dr. Ruscio's Leaky Gut Support Kit is a reasonable option. And if you just want one formula for repairing the gut lining, Designs for Health GI Revive is one of the more complete ones, but it's only for repair, it won't do the whole gut protocol for you.

I wouldn't recommend the general "gut cleanse" stacks (the ones built around oregano oil, wormwood, black walnut, berberine or other antimicrobial herbs) as a starting point for everyone. Those belong later on (Phase 3), once there's a stronger reason to suspect overgrowth, parasites, H. pylori or some other specific problem. (My own advice is different for H. pylori, where berberine works well: see Parasites, above.)

Start with low doses, especially of prebiotics, resistant starch, butyrate-support products and probiotics. And if you have severe pain, GI bleeding, fever, dehydration, rapid weight loss, an active IBD flare, cancer, immune suppression, a pregnancy, or another complex medical condition, don't stack supplements on your own, work with a qualified clinician instead.
